blocks.text: Every time your code runs, it does not always take the same amount of time. Sometimes it finishes in a single step, and sometimes it has to scan through the entire input.
The concepts of Best Case, Worst Case, and Average Case Complexity help describe how your algorithm behaves under different situations.
Once you understand this clearly, the symbols Ω (Omega), Θ (Theta), and O (Big-O) will no longer feel confusing they will simply become tools to describe algorithm performance.
Imagine you lost your phone somewhere in your house. There are 10 rooms, and you start searching room by room.
This simple example shows that an algorithm can behave differently depending on the situation, which is exactly why we analyze Best, Average, and Worst Case Complexity.
You have probably seen O, Ω, and Θ in textbooks and felt confused. In reality, they are simply ways to describe how many steps an algorithm can take.
Here is what each one means in plain language.
O( ):  Big O (Worst Case)
Big O describes the maximum number of steps your algorithm might take.
It represents the worst possible scenario. No matter what input you give, the algorithm will never be slower than this bound.
Think of Big O as the ceiling of your algorithm’s running time it cannot go above this limit.
Ω( ) : Omega (Best Case)
Omega describes the minimum number of steps your algorithm might take when everything goes perfectly.
It represents the best possible scenario, where the algorithm finds what it needs almost immediately.
Think of Omega as the floor the algorithm cannot do better than this.
Θ( ): Theta (Tight / Exact Bound)
Theta describes the actual growth of the algorithm when the upper and lower bounds meet.
It represents the most accurate description of how the algorithm behaves as the input grows.
You can think of Theta as the true behavior zone, where the algorithm’s performance is consistently bounded both above and below.
In short:

O( ) → Upper bound (worst case)
Ω( ) → Lower bound (best case)
Θ( ) → Tight bound (actual growth)

content.title: 2. Why Big O Is Used the Most

blocks.text: In interviews and real-world software development, people almost always talk about Big O notation the worst-case complexity.
The reason is simple: when you are building systems for thousands or even millions of users, you must understand the worst situation your algorithm might face.
You cannot design systems assuming everything will go perfectly. Instead, engineers plan for the maximum amount of work the algorithm might need to do.
That is why Big O focuses on the upper bound the largest number of steps the algorithm could take as the input grows.

In simple terms:
You design systems by preparing for the worst case, not the best case.
You have an array of numbers, and you want to find the number 7. You start checking the numbers one by one from the beginning.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785249011363-284355249.png

Best Case Ω(1)
If 7 is the first element, you find it immediately.
Only 1 step is needed.

Average Case Θ(n)
Most of the time, the number will be somewhere in the middle.
You check about half of the array before finding it.

Worst Case O(n)
If 7 is the last element or not in the array, you must check every number.
So in Linear Search:
The array is sorted, and you use Binary Search, which checks the middle element and halves the search space each step.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785249013126-235643093.png

- Best Case Ω(1)
The first middle element is the number you want.
You find it in one step.

- Average Case Θ(log n)
Usually, you need to halve the array a few times before finding the number.

- Worst Case O(log n)
Even in the worst situation, you only keep dividing the array in half, so it takes about log n steps.
So for Binary Search:

NOTICE SOMETHING INTERESTING

For Binary Search, best case is O(1) but worst and average are both O(log n). For Linear Search, best is O(1), average is O(n/2), worst is O(n). 

The same problem finding an element solved two ways gives you completely different complexity behaviour.

content.title: 5. Complexity Speed Chart (From Fastest to Slowest)

blocks.text:
Here is how common time complexities compare.
Imagine the input size is n = 1000 elements.
When n = 1000:

• O(n) ≈ 1,000 operations
  • O(n²) ≈ 1,000,000 operations
That jump is not just 2× slower it is 1000× slower.
This is why choosing the right algorithm matters. The difference between O(n) and O(n²) can mean the difference between a program that finishes in milliseconds and one that takes minutes.

blocks.text: The one thing that confuses everyone constants are dropped
Big O notation describes how an algorithm’s work grows as the input size grows. It does not try to show the exact number of steps, so we ignore constants and smaller terms.
For example, 3n + 5 is written as O(n). The +5 is a constant and becomes unimportant when n gets large. The 3 is also just a constant multiplier, so the growth is still linear.
Similarly, n² + n becomes O(n²) because n² grows much faster than n. As the input increases, the n² term dominates the running time.
If an algorithm always takes a fixed number of steps like 5, we write O(1). The exact number does not matter because the work does not grow with input size.
A common beginner mistake is writing O(2n) or O(n/2). In Big O notation, constants are ignored, so both are simply O(n). The main goal is to understand the growth pattern, not the exact step count.

content.title: 7. Why this matters when you write code

blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785249016413-486593698.png

Whenever you write a solution whether in a coding interview or in a real production system time complexity is one of the main things people evaluate. It determines how well your code scales as the input size grows.
Here’s what different complexities typically look like in practice when n becomes large:
O(1) or O(log n)
These scale extremely well, even for billions of operations. This is the ideal complexity for operations like lookups, indexing, and efficient searches.
O(n) or O(n log n)
These are perfectly acceptable for most real-world systems. Scanning through a dataset once or sorting millions of records is usually manageable at this complexity.
O(n²)

This can work for small inputs (typically a few thousand elements). But as the input grows, performance quickly degrades. In interviews, if your solution is O(n²) and the input size is large, the interviewer will almost always expect you to optimize it.
O(2ⁿ)

This grows extremely fast and is only feasible for very small inputs usually under 20. It often appears in naive recursive or backtracking solutions without optimization. When you encounter this, techniques like memoization or dynamic programming are usually required to make the solution practical.
